Draft:

Summer projects exist for a good reason. Anyone who has watched a classroom in September knows that two and a half months away from school can leave a student rusty in math, rusty in writing, and rusty in the habit of sitting down to think. But the question of who should design those projects matters just as much as whether to assign them. I believe summer projects should be student-designed, with teacher guidance built in at the start and the end.

The strongest argument for student design is motivation. A summer assignment competes with swimming pools, part-time jobs, family trips, and a hundred other things that feel more urgent. A teacher-designed packet of twenty worksheets rarely wins that contest. It arrives as an obligation, and students respond to obligations by doing the minimum, often in the last weekend of August. A project a student chose themselves has a chance of surviving the competition, because the student already cares about the answer. A girl who loves baking can spend the summer testing how altitude, humidity, and oven temperature change the rise of bread, and she will be doing real chemistry without once being told that is what she is doing. A boy who wants to build a skateboard ramp has to calculate angles, estimate lumber costs, and write down a budget. The learning is real because the goal is real.

Student design also teaches something a worksheet never can, which is how to plan. In college and at work, nobody hands people a list of problems with an answer key. They have to decide what to do, break it into steps, set deadlines, and notice when they are falling behind. Summer is the ideal time to practice that, because the stakes are low. If a student sets a goal that is too ambitious and has to scale back, they have learned something valuable about estimating their own time, and they have lost nothing but a few weeks of vacation. A teacher-designed project, by contrast, lets the student hand all of that thinking to someone else.

The obvious objection is that students will choose easy projects, or choose nothing at all. That is a fair worry, and it is why the teacher still has a role. A good system would ask each student to submit a short proposal in June, explaining what they plan to do, what they hope to learn, and how they will show the result. The teacher can approve it, push for more depth, or suggest a connection to the coming year's curriculum. A student who proposes to "watch documentaries" can be asked to write a review comparing three of them. A student who proposes to read a book can be asked to choose one above their usual level. Then, in the fall, the student presents the finished work to the class. The proposal and the presentation give the teacher control over standards without taking away the student's ownership.

Some will say that teacher-designed projects guarantee that everyone practices the same essential skills. But a summer assignment is a poor tool for that purpose anyway. Skills that matter, such as fractions, grammar, or reading comprehension, are better rebuilt in the first weeks of the school year, where a teacher can actually see who needs help. Summer should do something school cannot, which is let a young person pursue a question for its own sake.

If the goal of a summer project is to keep students learning, then the best project is the one a student will actually finish and care about. Letting students design their own, with a teacher checking the plan and the result, protects both rigor and interest. It also sends a message that learning does not stop when the bell rings, because it belongs to the learner.
